title: Multi-Level Resistive Synapses for On-Chip Neural Networks: A Physics-Based Design of a Memristive Crossbar Fabric with Quasi-Continuous Conductance States
abstract: Building on resistive communication, this paper presents a physics-based design of an on-chip neural network with multi-level memristive synapses supporting a dense spectrum of conductance states. Derived from ionic transport physics, we develop a state-variable model and quantify storable sub-levels under thermal noise, drift, and quantized conductance. We assemble these devices into a 1T1R crossbar fabric, derive the linear algebra of analog vector-matrix multiplication (VMM) under wire resistance, and design a differential synapse for signed weights. A multilayer pipeline executes inference, backpropagation, and weight updates physically in the analog domain. We derive the in-situ outer-product learning rule, its discretization onto the conductance lattice, and the resulting quantization noise. We provide energy, area, capacity, and inter-tile models, showing this substrate is ideally suited for large language models (LLMs). Our design eliminates weight movement, surpassing binary ReRAM and traditional CMOS. We detail the material stack (HfO_2-based), the FEOL/BEOL CMOS foundry-integration flow, a self-contained SPICE model, the complete memristive-FPGA neuromorphic system, and an in-memory self-attention engine with current-mode translinear softmax. Finally, a ternary BitNet datapath shows projected per-token efficiency orders of magnitude better than advanced CPUs or GPUs. The result is a self-contained hardware-native blueprint for a high-density, analog, in-memory neural processor.
summary: This work presents a comprehensive, physics-based blueprint for an in-memory neuromorphic processor using multi-level memristive synapses. By performing analog matrix multiplication directly where weights are stored, it bypasses the energy limitations of data movement inherent in conventional digital computing architectures. The resulting architecture is highly scalable and extremely energy efficient for modern AI workloads like LLMs.
main_problem: Overcoming the von Neumann bottleneck in data-intensive AI workloads by integrating memory and computation onto a single chip.
main_result: The proposed memristive crossbar fabric achieves energy efficiency orders of magnitude better than digital accelerators for LLM inference by performing MAC operations in the analog domain.
method: Developing physics-based models derived from ionic transport (Nernst–Planck) to characterize multi-level conductance states, and then applying these devices in a full neuromorphic architecture.
model_or_system: The system is a memristive crossbar fabric built using $	ext{HfO}_2$-based resistive synapses, capable of storing quasi-continuous analog weights. It implements computation via Kirchhoff's laws ($\mathbf{I} = \mathbf{G}^	op\mathbf{v}$) in the physical domain.
key_observables: Energy per token ($E_{	ext{tok}}$), Throughput ($	ext{tok}/	ext{s}$), Number of distinguishable conductance levels ($L_{th}$), and Output Current ($\mathbf{I}$).
important_parameters: Device parameters include the dynamic range ($ho = G_{max}/G_{min}$) and the read-noise floor ($\sigma G_{th}$); architectural scaling involves 3D stacking depth ($T$) and cell area ($a_{	ext{cell}}$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes that weight movement energy dominates digital costs, justifying the in-memory approach; performance figures are projections based on ideal device behavior.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the physical cross-section of 3D BEOL integration, the overall memristive-FPGA system architecture, and comparative roofline analyses showing superior scaling over digital methods.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from fundamental physics modeling (ionic transport) to device characterization (level count, noise), then details the analog computation primitives (VMM, self-attention), and concludes with architectural blueprints for full LLM inference engines.
why_interesting: While focused on AI hardware, the underlying physical modeling of state evolution ($\dot{x} = f(x, v)$) derived from charge/ion dynamics shares mathematical parallels with non-equilibrium statistical mechanics used to model complex material states.

Input voltages vi drive the rows; each junction memristor Gij injects a current Gijvi onto its column; Kirchhoff’s law sums them, and a transimpedance integrator reads Ij = P i Gijvi. The whole product I = G⊤v is computed in one step (Theorem 5.1).

Figure 7. Microscopic mechanism of bipolar resistive switching. Under +Vset mo- bile species (oxygen vacancies or metal cations, red) drift from the active electrode and nucleate a conductive filament across the oxide; the compliance current Icc caps its cross-section—and hence Gmax (18). A reverse −Vreset ruptures the filament, returning the cell toward the HRS. Partial set/reset stops the front at intermediate heights, realizing the analog sub-levels of Section 3; each such event is an act of resistive communication.

Figure 8. Neuristor built from two Mott memristors M1, M2, each shunted by a capacitance Ck and biased with opposite polarity. Crossing the insulator–metal transition voltage triggers an all-or-nothing relaxation spike at vout: the electronic action potential used as the spiking neuron at each tile output.

Figure 10. In-memory self-attention. Queries drive a volatile scratch crossbar holding K⊤to produce scores S (one VMM); a current-mode translinear stage com- putes the softmax; a second VMM against a volatile V crossbar yields the context AV. Diffusive (self-erasing) memristors serve as the KV scratch, avoiding non- volatile rewrite wear.
